answer: STRENGTHS: (1) Real, well-articulated problem: infrequent neurologist visits and subjective recall leave medication decisions based on snapshots; the gap in continuous movement-disorder monitoring is credible. (2) Founder-problem fit: the idea originated from direct clinic exposure by a neuroscience student, with complementary skills (clinical/product, engineering, operations). (3) Real traction signal for this stage: a working prototype (capture, scoring, clinician dashboard) and a paying pilot client, which is meaningful early validation of willingness to pay. (4) Sensible go-to-market: B2B sales to small/mid neurology practices with faster purchasing cycles, and a web app that suits older users with no download barrier. (5) Low deployment cost relative to hardware competitors (uses existing cameras); potential reimbursement tailwind via remote patient monitoring. (6) Honest self-awareness: founders openly name validation, reimbursement, regulatory, and team gaps, and the funding ask maps directly to those gaps. WEAKNESSES: (1) No clinical validation: accuracy of video-based tremor scoring versus clinical scales (e.g., MDS-UPDRS) or FDA-cleared wearables is unproven and is the core value proposition; without it, clinician trust and adoption are at risk. (2) Regulatory ambiguity: software that quantifies a symptom to inform treatment may qualify as a medical device (SaMD) requiring FDA consideration; no regulatory plan or expertise exists. (3) Privacy/compliance exposure: storing patient hand videos is PHI; HIPAA, BAAs, security, and consent requirements are unaddressed, and video storage costs are non-trivial. (4) Reimbursement is unconfirmed; the pricing and clinic ROI rest on unverified billing codes, and the clinic-pays model depends entirely on this. (5) Thin market sizing and weak financials: no bottom-up TAM, ~$50K ARR projection from 10 clinics/200 patients is small, untested assumptions, and unit economics (video storage vs. $15-25/patient/month) are not shown. (6) Patient adherence risk: daily self-recorded video from older, possibly cognitively affected patients may suffer high dropout, which undermines data quality; tremor is also only one of several Parkinson's symptoms, narrowing clinical value. (7) Team/organizational gaps: no physician or regulatory expert (only an informal advisor), no clinical research partner, legal entity and founder equity split unresolved, no website; student founders with limited runway and commitment post-graduation described but unproven. (8) Competitive defensibility is modest: computer-vision approach is replicable, incumbents have clinical validation and FDA clearance, and no moat (data, IP, validated algorithm) is yet established. OVERALL: Interesting, credible early-stage idea with genuine pilot traction and a clear problem, but high technical-validation, regulatory, and compliance risk plus unresolved company formation. Investment interest is moderate: worthy of small, milestone-driven support (validation study, legal setup) rather than substantial capital until clinical accuracy and reimbursement are demonstrated.
